title: Two Sum

understand.question: Given a list of whole numbers and a target total, which two different positions in the list add up to that exact target?
understand.plainExplanation: Imagine checking receipts to find two items whose prices add up to an exact gift-card balance. You cannot count the same receipt twice, and you must report the positions (indices) of the two chosen numbers, not the numbers themselves.
understand.inputMeaning: An integer array nums (for example [4, 9, 1, 7]) and an integer target (for example 10).
understand.outputMeaning: A two-element array [i, j] holding the 0-based positions of the two numbers where nums[i] + nums[j] == target and i != j.
rules: You must pick two distinct positions (you cannot reuse the same index twice, even if nums[i] * 2 == target).
The same numeric value can appear at two different positions and still be valid (e.g., [5, 5] with target 10 returns [0, 1]).
Every valid input has exactly one solution, and indices may be returned in any order.

terms.definition: A 0-based position in the array. The first number sits at index 0, the second at index 1, and so on.
The missing partner needed to reach target: complement = target - current_number.
A lookup table that stores key -> value pairs (here, number -> index) so we can check in roughly constant time whether a needed partner appeared earlier.

example1.whyValid: At index 1 we have 9 and at index 2 we have 1. Since 1 != 2 and 9 + 1 = 10, [1, 2] is the unique valid pair of indices.

diagram.caption: Positions 1 and 2 hold 9 and 1, which sum to target = 10.

example2.whyEdgeCase: Duplicate values and negative numbers! Notice 5 appears twice at indices 1 and 2. You cannot pair index 1 with itself, so a hash map must avoid matching an element against its own index, and negative numbers like -3 can be present.

steps.title: Initialize empty lookup table
steps.description: Start at index 0 with an empty hash map seen = {}. For each number x, we only need to check if target - x (10 - x) is already inside seen.

steps.title: Index 0 (value 4): store in map
steps.description: Complement 10 - 4 = 6 is not in seen. Store 4 -> 0 so future elements can pair with it, then advance i to 1.

steps.title: Index 1 (value 9): store in map
steps.description: Complement 10 - 9 = 1 is not in seen yet. Store 9 -> 1 and advance i to 2.

steps.title: Index 2 (value 1): complement 9 found!
steps.description: 10 - 1 = 9 IS in seen at index 1! Because we check seen BEFORE inserting nums[2], indices 1 and 2 are guaranteed to be distinct. Return [1, 2].

approaches.name: Brute Force Nested Loops
approaches.coreIdeaSummary: Check every distinct pair (i, j) with i < j.
approaches.coreIdea: Try every pair of distinct positions (i, j) with j > i and return as soon as nums[i] + nums[j] equals target.
steps: For each i, loop j from i + 1 to n - 1.
If nums[i] + nums[j] == target, return [i, j].
approaches.whyItWorks: Iterating over all pairs with i < j checks every valid two-index combination exactly once without ever pairing an index with itself.
approaches.whenToUse: Use as a baseline sanity check or when memory is tightly constrained (O(1) extra space) and n is small.
approaches.diagramNote: Outer pointer i stays fixed while inner pointer j scans every position to its right.

approaches.name: Two-Pass Hash Map
approaches.coreIdeaSummary: Index all values first, then look up each element's complement.
approaches.coreIdea: Build a value-to-index map in a first pass, then scan the array a second time checking whether target - nums[i] exists at a different index.
steps: Pass 1: insert every nums[i] -> i into a hash map.
Pass 2: for each index i, compute complement = target - nums[i].
If complement is in the map and map[complement] != i, return [i, map[complement]].
approaches.whyItWorks: Even if duplicates exist, Pass 1 stores the latest index for a value while Pass 2 starts from index 0, so map[complement] != i still finds the second copy cleanly.
approaches.whenToUse: Helpful when separating index construction from querying makes code easier to reason about.
approaches.diagramNote: Pass 1 indexes every number; Pass 2 queries need = 10 - nums[i] and confirms j != i.

diagram.caption: Pass 2 at i=1 looks up 10 - 9 = 1 -> index 2.

approaches.name: Sort + Two Pointers
approaches.coreIdeaSummary: Sort (value, originalIndex) pairs and walk inward from both ends.
approaches.coreIdea: Pair each value with its original index, sort by value, and move left/right pointers inward based on whether the current sum is too small or too large.
steps: Build pairs (nums[i], i) for all i.
Sort the pairs in non-decreasing order by value.
Set left = 0, right = n - 1. While left < right, compute sum = pairs[left].val + pairs[right].val.
If sum == target, return the two original indices; if sum < target, increment left; else decrement right.
approaches.whyItWorks: Because the pairs are sorted by value, increasing left strictly cannot decrease the sum and decreasing right strictly cannot increase it, guaranteeing we never skip the valid pair.
approaches.whenToUse: Great when the input is already sorted (eliminating the O(n log n) sort and O(n) pairing) or as the foundation for 3Sum and 4Sum.
approaches.diagramNote: Pairs (value, originalIndex) are sorted by value so left/right pointers squeeze inward toward target 10.

diagram.caption: After sorting (val@origIdx), L=0 and R=3 sum to 10.

approaches.name: Sort + Binary Search
approaches.coreIdeaSummary: Sort (value, index) pairs and binary-search the complement for each position.
approaches.coreIdea: After sorting value-index pairs, iterate through each position i and binary-search the suffix [i + 1 .. n - 1] for target - pairs[i].val.
steps: Store (nums[i], i) pairs and sort by value.
For each sorted index i from 0 to n - 2, binary-search in [i + 1, n - 1] for need = target - pairs[i].val.
If found at mid, return [pairs[i].idx, pairs[mid].idx].
approaches.whyItWorks: Sorting makes every suffix [i + 1 .. n - 1] monotonic, so binary search checks for the partner in O(log n) without revisiting index i.
approaches.whenToUse: Useful when worst-case O(n log n) predictability matters more than expected O(n) hash performance.
approaches.diagramNote: Fix sorted entry i=0 (value 1) and binary-search suffix [1..3] for 10 - 1 = 9.

diagram.caption: Binary search halves [1..3] until landing on 9@1.

approaches.name: One-Pass Hash Map
approaches.recommendedTradeOff: Trades O(n) extra hash table memory to cut runtime from O(n^2) to expected O(n) in a single left-to-right scan, while naturally preventing self-pairing.
approaches.coreIdeaSummary: Check if target - nums[i] was already seen before inserting nums[i].
approaches.coreIdea: Maintain a hash map of numbers seen so far and their indices. At index i, immediately query whether target - nums[i] is already stored; if not, record nums[i] -> i.
steps: Create an empty hash map seen (value -> index).
Iterate i from 0 to n - 1 and compute complement = target - nums[i].
If complement exists in seen, return [seen[complement], i].
Otherwise insert seen[nums[i]] = i and continue.
approaches.whyItWorks: For any valid pair (a, b) with a < b, when the loop reaches b, nums[a] has already been placed into seen. Checking seen before inserting nums[b] also guarantees a != b even when nums[a] == nums[b].
approaches.whenToUse: Default choice for unsorted arrays whenever O(n) auxiliary space is acceptable.

complexity.boundType: Expected (worst-case O(n^2) only under adversarial hash collisions)

code.Erlang:
-spec two_sum(Nums :: [integer()], Target :: integer()) -> [integer()].
two_sum(Nums, Target) ->
  two_sum(Nums, Target, 0, #{}).

two_sum([H | T], Target, I, Seen) ->
  case maps:find(Target - H, Seen) of
    {ok, Prev} -> [Prev, I];
    error -> two_sum(T, Target, I + 1, maps:put(H, I, Seen))
  end.
code.Racket:
(define/contract (two-sum nums target)
  (-> (listof exact-integer?) exact-integer? (listof exact-integer?))
  (let loop ([rest nums] [i 0] [seen (hash)])
    (if (null? rest)
        '()
        (let* ([x (car rest)]
               [need (- target x)]
               [prev (hash-ref seen need #f)])
          (if prev
              (list prev i)
              (loop (cdr rest) (+ i 1) (hash-set seen x i)))))))
